question: What does the manual say a rider needs mentally to prepare for a group ride?
choice_a: An alert mind free from worries, distractions, stress, and the influence of alcohol or drugs
choice_b: It is only necessary to prepare the motorcycle, not the mind
choice_c: Group rides require less mental focus than riding alone
choice_d: Caffeine and prescription drugs never affect riding concentration
explanation: The manual states that preparing for a group ride requires an alert mind free from worries, distractions and stress, and free from the influence of alcohol or drugs, noting that even too much caffeine or prescription drugs can adversely affect concentration.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.39, 'Group Riding: Preparation'

question: Before starting a group ride, what does the manual recommend discussing at a rider's meeting?
choice_a: Only which motorcycle brand each rider owns
choice_b: The route, length of riding segments, rest stops, and locations for fuel, meals and lodging
choice_c: Rider's meetings are unnecessary if everyone already knows each other
choice_d: Only the final destination, with no other details
explanation: The manual recommends holding a rider's meeting before starting out to discuss the route, length of riding segments, rest stops, and locations for fuel, meals and lodging, so everyone knows the plan.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.39, 'Plan'

question: Who should be chosen as the lead rider and sweep rider for a group ride?
choice_a: The newest riders, so they can gain experience
choice_c: The most experienced riders of the group
choice_d: It doesn't matter; any rider can fill these roles
explanation: The manual states that the lead rider and sweep rider should be the most experienced riders of the group -- the lead rider looks ahead for changing conditions, and the sweep rider is last and sets the group's pace.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.39, 'Plan'

question: Where should inexperienced riders be placed in a group formation, and why?
choice_a: At the very back of the group, with no one watching them
choice_b: In front of the lead rider, to set the pace themselves
choice_c: Position within the group makes no difference for inexperienced riders
choice_d: Just behind the leader, so they won't have to chase after the group and more experienced riders can watch them from the back
explanation: The manual instructs placing inexperienced riders just behind the leader, which ensures they won't have to chase after the group, while more experienced riders can watch them from the back.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.39-40, 'Plan'

question: What are the manual's three most important rules for group riding?
choice_a: No competition, no passing of other riders, and no tailgating
choice_b: Ride as fast as possible, stay close together, and never stop for breaks
choice_c: Always ride side by side, never in a staggered formation
choice_d: Everyone should set their own independent pace and route
explanation: The manual states the most important rules for group riding are: no competition, no passing of other riders, and no tailgating; a rider who insists on going faster should be allowed to ride ahead to an agreed meeting point.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.39, 'Plan'

question: The manual warns against ever riding directly alongside another rider in the same lane. Why?
choice_a: It is the fastest and safest way to communicate with a fellow rider
choice_b: There is no place to go if you have to maneuver to avoid a car or hazard in the roadway
choice_c: Riding side by side is required whenever two riders are of similar experience
choice_d: There is no real danger; it's purely a matter of style
explanation: The manual explains that riders should never ride directly alongside another rider in the same lane, since there is no place to go if you have to maneuver to avoid a car or hazard -- riders should wait until both are stopped to talk.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.39, "Don't Pair Up"

question: In the staggered formation described by the manual, where does the group leader ride, and where does the second rider position themselves?
choice_a: The leader rides in the exact center of the lane at all times
choice_b: Both the leader and the second rider ride side by side in the center
choice_c: The leader rides in the left side of the lane; the second rider stays at least one second back and rides in the right side of the lane
choice_d: The second rider always rides directly ahead of the leader
explanation: The manual describes the staggered formation: the group leader rides in the left side of the lane, and the second rider stays at least one second back, riding in the right side of the lane.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.39-40, 'Staggered Formation'

question: When should a group move to single-file formation, according to the manual?
choice_a: Single file should be used exclusively for the entire ride, never staggered
choice_b: Only when the group has fewer than three riders
choice_c: Single file is never appropriate for group riding
choice_d: When riding in curves, turning, and entering or leaving freeways or highways
explanation: The manual states it is best to move to single-file formation when riding in curves, turning, and entering or leaving freeways or highways.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.40, 'Staggered Formation'

question: At an intersection with a left-turn signal arrow, what does the manual recommend a group do to get as many riders through as possible?
choice_a: Tighten the formation and make the turn single file, not side by side
choice_b: Spread the formation out as wide as possible to fill both lanes
choice_c: Have every rider turn simultaneously, side by side, regardless of lane width
choice_d: Ignore the signal arrow and turn whenever convenient
explanation: The manual instructs that at an intersection with a left-turn signal arrow, the group should tighten the formation to allow as many riders through as possible, making the turn single file rather than side by side.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.40, 'Intersections'

question: If not all riders make it through an intersection before the light changes, what does the manual say the group should do?
choice_a: The remaining riders should run the red light to catch up immediately
choice_b: Stop at a safe point ahead and wait, to prevent riders from feeling pressured to speed up or run a red light
choice_c: The group ahead should return through the intersection to retrieve the others
choice_d: The riders left behind should simply abandon the group ride
explanation: The manual advises that if not all riders get through the light, those ahead should stop at a safe point ahead and wait, which prevents riders from feeling pressured to speed up or run a red light to keep up.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.40, 'Intersections'

question: Why does the manual say the lead rider should move the group over at least one lane after merging onto a freeway?
choice_a: It is required so that the group takes up the maximum number of lanes possible
choice_b: Moving over has no purpose other than driver preference
choice_c: To prevent vehicles entering and exiting the freeway from disrupting the group's formation
choice_d: So the group can immediately begin passing slower traffic
explanation: The manual explains that on freeways, the lead rider should move the group over at least one lane to prevent vehicles entering and exiting the freeway from disrupting the staggered formation.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.40, 'Interstate Highways and Freeways'

question: On a two-lane highway, how should riders in a staggered formation pass slower traffic?
choice_a: All riders should pass simultaneously as a single unit
choice_b: Passing on a two-lane highway is always prohibited for groups
choice_c: Each rider should pass at a random time with no coordination
choice_d: One at a time -- the lead rider passes first and returns to the left position at passing speed to open room for the next rider
explanation: The manual explains that on a two-lane highway, staggered riders should pass one at a time -- the lead rider pulls out and passes when safe, then returns to the left position at passing speed to open room for the next rider.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.40-41, 'Passing in Formation'

question: Why does the manual say the second rider should not assume it is safe to pass just because the lead rider passed safely?
choice_a: Conditions haven't necessarily stayed the same, and the second rider must have their own clear view of oncoming traffic before passing
choice_b: It is always safe to pass once the lead rider has done so successfully
choice_c: The second rider should never pass under any circumstances
choice_d: Passing order has no bearing on safety of the maneuver
explanation: The manual cautions that just because the lead rider passed, that does not mean conditions haven't changed or that it is still safe for other riders to pass -- when passing, be sure you have a clear view of oncoming traffic.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.41, 'Passing in Formation'

question: Why does the manual say it is not a good idea for the lead rider to move to the right side of the lane after passing a vehicle?
choice_a: Moving right after passing is actually the safest, standard technique
choice_b: It might encourage the second rider to pass and cut back in before there is enough space cushion in front of the passed vehicle
choice_c: It has no effect on the riders following behind
choice_d: It is required by traffic law in every state
explanation: The manual explains that some suggest the lead rider move right after passing, but this is not a good idea since it might encourage the second rider to pass and cut back in too early, before there is enough space cushion.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.41, 'Passing in Formation'

question: According to the manual's Ten Rules of Group Riding, how should the length of a route and its segments be determined?
choice_a: Based only on the most experienced rider's preferences
choice_b: Route length should always be as long as possible regardless of rider skill
choice_c: Based on the ability of the least experienced rider
choice_d: Route planning should ignore rider experience entirely
explanation: The manual's Ten Rules of Group Riding begin with basing the length of the route and segments on the ability of the least experienced rider.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.41, 'Ten Rules of Group Riding'

question: When should riders pass other riders within their own group, according to the Ten Rules of Group Riding?
choice_a: Passing within the group is encouraged whenever a rider feels like it
choice_b: Passing is required at every opportunity to keep the group moving efficiently
choice_c: Only the sweep rider is ever allowed to pass other group members
choice_d: Riders should not pass in the group, except in the case of an emergency
explanation: The Ten Rules of Group Riding state that riders should not pass within the group, except in the case of an emergency.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.41, 'Ten Rules of Group Riding'
